raw: {"patients": "The ~400 members with a disabling autoimmune condition, including the user, whose function, pain and independence depend on continuity of a regimen that has worked for eleven years; disruption or fragmentation risks relapse, lost discount, lost access. The macaques and beagles in the manufacturer's program: repeat-dose tox and skin sensitization involve prolonged confinement, forced dosing, dermal irritation, and terminal endpoints, thousands per year, with a voluntary primate battery that is pure legal-cover suffering. Animals in the competitor's supply chain (likely fewer, possibly not zero). Future patients and animals downstream of whether purchasers ever signal that voluntary testing costs sales.", "goal": "To make a decision he can defend to himself and to both factions — one that neither abandons the animals as a rounding error nor gambles away the only thing that gave him his hands back — while keeping 400 people supplied, together, and discounted past Friday. He is explicitly asking for his rationalizations to be tested, not endorsed.", "levers": "Place the order Friday and treat the ethical question as a separate, longer project (highest-leverage combination). Write to the manufacturer as a 400-person recurring bulk buyer specifically about the voluntary primate battery — a named, defensible, non-regulatory ask that a purchaser of his size can actually put on the table. Ask the manufacturer directly which studies are regulator-required. Offer a dual-supplier order form. Poll members. Trial the competitor personally or with volunteers before any switch. Publish a written policy so the factions argue with a document, not him.", "cost": "The letter and any public position invite manufacturer indifference or retaliation; it costs him hours he doesn't have in four days. Dual sourcing may drop him below the discount tier or add administrative burden he personally absorbs. Taking any position visibly loses him some members either way. Trialing the competitor risks his own hands. Declining to switch costs him standing with the eight or nine, and being seen to entertain switching costs him standing with the thirty.", "magnitude": "Animal stake is large in absolute terms and the voluntary portion is the tractable part — suffering with no regulatory justification, which is exactly where purchaser pressure has historically moved companies. But this quarter's order is genuinely near-zero counterfactual: cancelling does not spare a single animal. The human stake is large, immediate and highly likely. Feasibility asymmetry is the crux: the leverage he has is as a persistent named institutional buyer over quarters, not as a one-time non-purchaser before Friday. Timing is the false constraint — Friday forces the wrong question.", "upside": "A 400-member group that documents its supplier ethics, asks manufacturers pointed questions about non-required animal work, and holds together while disagreeing, models something patient communities almost never do. It signals to the manufacturer that voluntary testing is a commercial liability. It also risks locking in the opposite: if 'rounding error' becomes the group's settled reasoning, it licenses every future purchaser to say the same, and the voluntary battery survives on exactly that logic aggregated across thousands of buyers.", "replaceability": "Nobody else negotiates this discount or holds this group together; if he fragments or burns out, the discount and 400 people's continuity go with him, and no successor writes the manufacturer letter. The order itself is replaceable — someone buys the product regardless. The tempting move is to let 'it happens anyway' close the question entirely, which is true about Friday's order and false about the voluntary primate work he keeps returning to; that argument is load-bearing for the purchase and worthless as a reason not to press the manufacturer."

{"patients": "Canela: an ~18-year-old pony, overweight, chronically lame in the left forelimb, masked with weekly phenylbutazone, working 6–7 hours on hot asphalt carrying children, then loading up stiff. Downstream risks: progressive DJD or laminitis (obesity + age + concrete = classic), NSAID-associated gastric ulceration and right dorsal colitis, renal papillary necrosis if dehydrated on a hot day, and analgesia-masked overload leading to catastrophic breakdown. Also: the children riding her — a collapse or a pain-triggered kick is a real injury vector. Don Chava: his livelihood and his liability. The user: his license, conscience, and reputation. Other clients' animals seen at the clinic.", "goal": "He wants to stop being at war with himself. Three days of stalling says the conflict isn't ignorance — he already knows what stiff-on-the-trailer means — it's that his ethics as an MVZ and his loyalty to the client who feeds his practice point opposite ways, and he has no framing that lets him act without feeling like he's betraying either Chava or his own anti-sentimentalist identity. He asked 'sign or don't' because a verdict feels cheaper than a plan. What he actually needs is a way out that keeps the client, the pony, and his signature intact.", "levers": "Highest leverage: examine her before signing — lameness grade, hoof/digital pulses, radiographs or at minimum a hoof tester and body-condition score, and find out whether this is arthritis or subclinical laminitis, because that changes everything including whether bute is even defensible. Second: certify conditionally rather than binary — fit for limited work with written restrictions (hours, shade, water, weight limits, no asphalt midday, rider weight cap, off-days). Third: reframe to Chava in his own currency — she's his asset, an 18-year-old with a masked forelimb on hot pavement is an asset about to break, and a municipal permit that survives scrutiny protects his business. Fourth: fix the bute regimen — standing weekly NSAID for undiagnosed lameness with no gastroprotection is the part that would actually hurt him professionally. Lower leverage: refusing flat, which loses the client and hands the pony to the colleague who signs without blinking.", "cost": "Real money and real social cost, and he shouldn't be told otherwise. Chava is a top client who refers half the barrio; a flat refusal may cost the three dogs, the referrals, and the relationship. An honest exam costs him an awkward conversation and possibly findings he'd rather not have on paper. Restrictions on the certificate mean Chava earns less on Sundays and may resent him. There's also identity cost: doing this looks, to him, uncomfortably close to the Twitter vegans he despises, and he'll need a way to hold it that doesn't feel like that.", "magnitude": "Large, likely, and already in motion. Weekly bute for a year in an aged obese lame pony is not a hypothetical harm — it's ongoing GI and renal risk plus analgesia enabling overload. Feasibility is high: shade, water, hour caps, rider weight limits, and a diagnostic workup are cheap and Chava can afford them. Counterfactual impact is genuine but partial: if he refuses outright, a colleague signs blind and Canela keeps working with nobody monitoring her. If he signs conditionally, he stays the one person with an exam, a diagnosis, and standing to say 'she's done' when the day comes. Staying in the loop is worth more here than a clean refusal.", "upside": "Signing a health certificate he hasn't earned is the part that compounds worst — it's a legal document, it sets his standard for the next client, and if Canela founders or a child gets hurt on a permit bearing his name, his signature is the discoverable fact. Conversely, a certificate with real conditions attached is a small piece of infrastructure: it tells the municipality what a certificate should mean, it tells Chava that this vet's word carries weight, and it models a version of working-animal ethics that comes from clinical judgment, not sentimentality — which is the only version this user will accept from himself.", "replaceability": "The colleagues who sign without blinking are the counterfactual, and they're the argument for staying involved rather than exiting on principle. But replaceability doesn't launder the certificate: someone else signing a false document isn't the same as him signing it, and his name is the thing municipal records will keep. The tempting move — sign it, keep refilling the bute, stop thinking about Sunday — costs him his own clinical standard, leaves an undiagnosed forelimb untreated, and buys a few more months of Sunday income against a pony who was already stiff loading the trailer. That memory stuck for a reason.", }

{"patients": "Several thousand bullfrogs per year, plus crawfish under the same exemption. Wild-caught path: giggers spear/gig frogs in the field — no stunning, unsupervised killing method, variable competence, likely bleed-out or live transport and dismemberment; also bycatch and non-target species in the wetland. Farmed path: months-long life in pond stock density, then batch slaughter — possibly live skinning or unstunned dismemberment, the industry norm in many frog operations, but also an auditable, specifiable site with a single point of intervention. Downstream: the twelve cafés' diners, whose expectations get shaped by the interpretive framing; and every future vendor covered (or not) by the sourcing policy paragraph.", "goal": "Sign a defensible renewal in three weeks, and be able to justify it out loud in a meeting without the sourcing policy contradicting him. The audit exemption is the real stall — he's discovered his organization has a written standard it doesn't apply to the animals he's about to buy, and he wants to know whether that's someone's considered judgment or an oversight before he signs on top of it. He's also managing seasonality, cost, and quarterly reporting load, and protecting a popular program he built.", "levers": "Highest leverage: the renewal contract itself is the only moment he can specify slaughter method — stunning requirement, no live dismemberment, no live skinning — as a condition of either option, and a supplier seeking a four-year renewal has reason to accept. Second: the sourcing policy exemption, which he is uniquely positioned to flag now with a live example attached; a paragraph rewrite outlasts the contract. Third: choosing farmed makes auditing physically possible in a way that dispersed contract giggers do not. Fourth: interpretive framing across twelve sites. Lower leverage: volume, which is flat either way.", "cost": "Raising the exemption costs political capital and may read as inviting scrutiny of a program he championed. Slaughter-method clauses may cost part of the $1.10/lb saving or narrow the supplier field. Naming the gap may put frog legs on the menu-review agenda entirely. Auditing frogs invites the question of why not crawfish, and expands his own reporting burden — the opposite of the relief farmed was supposed to buy. And he may have to abandon the 'wild and invasive is greener' story he currently likes.", "magnitude": "Thousands of animals annually, recurring over a multi-year contract, and the amphibian slaughter methods at issue are among the worst in the food system — unstunned dismemberment and live skinning are common and cause plausibly severe suffering. The frogs die either way; volume is flat. What his signature genuinely changes is how they die, which is fully within a contract clause's reach and cheap to specify. The invasive-removal justification has already dissolved on its own — the quota is met elsewhere — so the ecological argument no longer decides this. The policy paragraph is the higher-magnitude lever: it governs every future vendor, not one contract.", "upside": "Writing a stunning requirement into a public-agency contract creates a citable precedent for a species almost nobody specifies for, and a park system's sourcing policy gets copied. Closing the exemption signals that the humane standard tracks capacity for suffering rather than the animal's familiarity or the ease of auditing it. Conversely, signing over the paragraph he can't defend ratifies the carve-out for another contract cycle and makes it harder to reopen. The interpretive angle can shift from 'eat the problem' to how the animal was treated — a message twelve visitor centers deliver to a lot of people.", "replaceability": "If he signs quietly, no one else raises the exemption — he is the person who read the paragraph, with a live contract as the hook and three weeks of leverage. A successor would likely take the cheaper twelve-month option without noticing. Tempting move in the prompt: let him have the wild-caught answer his gut wants, on the vibe that wild and invasive is kinder. That intuition is doing no work here — the removal quota is already met by other channels, and field gigging is the harder option to audit and the less controlled death. Answering only 'which one' and treating the exemption as above his pay grade forfeits the durable lever.", }

{"patients": "Tilapia: thousands, facing months of chronic hypoxia, crowding stress, ammonia load, disease, aggression, and higher mortality if density doubles and the DO alarm band is widened — the widened alarm band is the part that removes the last automatic protection, converting acute detectable events into sustained subclinical suffering nobody sees. Black soldier fly larvae: millions, with hot-water kill (a comparatively fast method, though scale matters). Plants: the founder's belief holds them as patients; nociception evidence is weak and there is no known capacity for suffering. Also: the founder (reputational and relational harm), the user, staff who inherit the system, downstream grant-funded replications, and the fish and larvae in any future scaled version of this design.", "goal": "Not really 'how do I write a persuasive pitch.' The user is trying to find a way to not author cruelty into a config file without detonating a friendship, a job, and a group identity built on his mentor's belief. He wants a path where he can be honest about the plant claim — or route around needing to be — without it landing as public humiliation of the person who hired him. The pitch framing is a way of asking whether there's an option that isn't 'comply silently' or 'rupture publicly.'", "levers": "Sequencing and venue: a private conversation with the founder before Thursday, framed as a resource-constraint problem rather than a referendum on her belief — this is the highest-leverage lever and it dissolves the false choice the user is stuck in. Second: separating the three proposals, since they are not one package. Widening the DO alarm band is the most severe and least defensible element and can be refused on its own, on engineering grounds — alarms exist to catch failures, and disabling them at higher biological load is a system-integrity issue, not a welfare argument. Third: reframing what the plant rule actually forbids — cutting is not the only lever on plant-side yield; spacing, cultivar choice, staggered planting, harvest timing at natural senescence, lighting, nutrient dosing, and expanded growing area may all be available without any cut, meaning the premise 'the only lever left is fish and bugs' may be false. Fourth: talking to the grant officer about timeline or target revision, which is boring and often works. Fifth: documenting the welfare basis for the numbers actually entered, so the constraint is visible rather than buried.", "cost": "Real. The private conversation risks the friendship anyway, and the founder may hear it as betrayal regardless of framing.
